The classical age of the Japanese imperial court, from 710 to 1185. It began when the court settled at Nara, the first fixed capital, and ran through the Heian period, named for Heian-kyo, modern Kyoto, where the capital moved in 794.

Nara (710 to 794). The state was modelled on Tang China, with a law code, the Taiho Code, provinces and taxes in rice and labour. Buddhism was the state's protector. Emperor Shomu built the Great Buddha of Todai-ji, and the Kojiki, Japan's oldest chronicle, was written in 712. A smallpox epidemic in 735 to 737 may have killed a third of the people.

Heian (794 to 1185). Chinese influence faded and a native court culture grew.

  • The kana scripts, hiragana and katakana, made it easy to write Japanese.
  • Court women wrote the great works in it, above all Murasaki Shikibu's Tale of Genji.
  • Kukai and others founded new Buddhist schools, such as Shingon and Tendai at Mount Hiei.

Real power lay with the Fujiwara clan, who married their daughters to emperors and ruled as regents. Meanwhile private estates grew outside the tax system, and provincial warrior families rose to protect them. In the 12th century two of these, the Taira and the Minamoto, fought the Genpei War. Minamoto no Yoritomo won in 1185 and set up the Kamakura shogunate, beginning seven centuries of warrior rule.
sum: The classical age of the Japanese imperial court, from 710 to 1185. It began when the court settled at Nara, the first fixed capital, and ran through the Heian period, named for Heian-kyo, modern Kyoto, where the capital moved in 794.
